A light string attached to the cart passes over a light frictionless pulley at the end of the track and is attached to a hanging block of mass $m$. The system is released from rest. Divides only by the cart mass and forgets that the hanging mass also accelerates.

ap_physics_1-m03.stem: A $20\text{ kg}$ lamp hangs at rest from two light ropes attached to the same ceiling. Each rope makes an angle of $20^\circ$ with the horizontal on opposite sides of the lamp. Which statement about the tension in each rope is correct and best justified?

options.text: The tension in each rope is $98.0\text{ N}$, because the two ropes share the weight equally.
options.why: Splits the weight equally without noting that each rope pulls at an angle, so the vertical component is only part of the tension.

options.text: The tension in each rope is $287\text{ N}$, which is greater than half of the weight ($98.0\text{ N}$), because only the vertical component of each tension supports the lamp.
options.why: The vertical components must sum to the weight: $2T\sin20^\circ=196\text{ N}$, so $T=287\text{ N}$, which is more than $W/2$.

options.text: The tension in each rope is $196\text{ N}$, because each rope must by itself balance the weight of the lamp.
options.why: Assumes that each rope supports the full weight, ignoring the other rope.

options.text: The tension in each rope is $104\text{ N}$, because the horizontal components of the tensions support the lamp.
options.why: Uses the horizontal component to support the weight; the horizontal components cancel each other.

blueprint.subject: ap_physics_1
blueprint.concept: Justifying the tension in two angled ropes from the vertical balance of forces
student_thinking: Resolve each tension into vertical and horizontal components
Set the sum of the vertical components equal to the weight

key_conditions.condition: the lamp is at rest and the ropes are symmetric
key_conditions.evidence: the stem says the lamp hangs at rest and the ropes make equal angles

misconceptions.description: Splits the weight equally without noting that each rope pulls at an angle, so the vertical component is only part of the tension.
Assumes that each rope supports the full weight, ignoring the other rope.
Uses the horizontal component to support the weight; the horizontal components cancel each other.

verification.independent_path: a linear solve of the horizontal and vertical force balance gives equal tensions greater than half the weight

ap_physics_1-m04.stem: A student pulls a cart on a low-friction track with several different constant net forces and measures the acceleration each time. The table shows the net force and the acceleration for five trials. Which of the following is best supported by the data?

stimulus.description: Net force and acceleration of a cart

options.text: The product $Fa$ is nearly constant, so a larger force gives a smaller acceleration.
options.why: Tests the product, but the product increases with the force.

options.text: The ratio $F/a$ is nearly the same in every trial, about $4.01\text{ kg}$, so the data support an acceleration proportional to the net force with a cart mass of about $4.01\text{ kg}$.
options.why: The ratios $F/a$ range only from $3.93$ to $4.07\text{ kg}$, so $a\propto F$ and the ratio is the mass.

options.text: The acceleration is nearly the same in every trial, so it does not depend on the net force.
options.why: Overlooks that the acceleration rises from $0.254\text{ m/s}^2$ to $1.965\text{ m/s}^2$ as the force increases.

options.text: The ratio $a/F$ is nearly the same in every trial, about $0.250\text{ kg}$, so this ratio is the mass of the cart.
options.why: Takes the reciprocal ratio $a/F$ as the mass, but the mass is $F/a$.

blueprint.concept: Supporting Newton's second law with the ratio of force to acceleration computed from a data table
student_thinking: Compute $F/a$ for each trial
Decide what a nearly constant ratio says about the acceleration and the mass

key_conditions.condition: the net force is constant during each trial
key_conditions.evidence: the stem says constant net forces are used

misconceptions.description: Tests the product, but the product increases with the force.

ap_physics_1-m20.stem: Two objects A and B have the same volume of $3\text{ L}$ but different masses ($3\text{ kg}$ and $9\text{ kg}$). Each object is held completely underwater in a large tank of water by a thin light string attached to the bottom of the tank. Which statement about the buoyant forces on the objects is correct and best justified?

options.text: The buoyant force on each object equals its own weight, because both objects are at rest.
options.why: Sets the buoyant force equal to the weight even though the string also pulls on each object.

options.text: The buoyant forces are equal ($29.4\text{ N}$ each), because each object displaces the same volume of water.
options.why: The buoyant force is $\rho_{water}gV=(1000)(9.8)(0.003)=29.4\text{ N}$ for both objects.

options.text: The buoyant force on B is greater, because B has more mass and is pulled down harder.
options.why: Ties the buoyant force to the mass of the object rather than to the weight of the displaced fluid.

options.text: The buoyant force on A is greater, because A is less dense and floats better.
options.why: Confuses a tendency to float with the size of the buoyant force; both are fully submerged with equal displaced volume.
